newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FOCUS - Portugal wrong-foots markets on rate.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Portugal wrong-foots markets on rate.

text.p: The Bank of Portugal wrong-footed the financial markets on Friday -- not cutting a key interest rate as expected -- but analysts said that it was just a matter of time before it did.
The central bank had been widely expected to reduce its drain rate, the rate at which it absorbs excess money market funds, by at least 0.20 percent from its current 6.2 percent.
Seven out of nine analysts polled by Reuters on Thursday had predicted a cut.
Spain lowered a key market rate on Thursday, and this together with the strength of the Portuguese escudo and inflation figures in line with expectations were seen as giving the Bank room to move.
But there was no change when the central bank announced the conditions for the next commercial bank reserve period beginning on Monday.
The bond market, which had been gaining on expectations of a rate cut, took the decision in its stride and was trading little changed late afternoon from Thursday's close.

"All the conditions are there for a rate cut but the Bank opted for caution. Perhaps it is waiting for better inflation numbers and does not want to appear to be following Spain," said one bond market trader.
Spain's central bank cut its repurchase pact rate by 0.25 percent on Thursday to 6.0 percent.
Although Portugal's inflation rate finished 1996 in line with government forecasts, with the rolling 12-month average, the benchmark rate, at 3.1 percent, the year-on-year level quickened slightly.

The year-on-year rate rose in December to 3.3 percent from 3.0 percent the previous month. Economists and government officials have warned that there could be a further rise in the early months of 1997.
But the officials and independent economists expect the rate to slow again from April or May onwards, with Portugal still on track to meet its end-1997 goal of average inflation under 2.5 percent.
"The Bank has opted for caution at a moment in which the inflation rate looked like rising in January and February," said Banco Portugues de Investimento (BPI) chief economist Rui Martins dos Santos.
"(But) there continues to be room for rates to come down," he said.
